items.title: Could JAPAN discover life on Mars?! #shorts
items.summary: Let’s say hello to the Martian Moon exploration mission or MMX, which launched from Tanegashima Island in the early hours of 20th October 2026. This is a Japanese space agency mission, with some colla…
items.body:
Let’s say hello to the Martian Moon exploration mission or MMX, which launched from Tanegashima Island in the early hours of 20th October 2026. This is a Japanese space agency mission, with some collaboration with NASA and ESA, that it set to study Mars’s two moons Phobos and Deimos, and return samples from Phobos.

And this is a big deal, because despite landing nine spacecraft on Mars over the past 50 years, we’ve never brought back samples. The Perseverance rover has been collecting samples and leaving them on the surface for the planned Mars Sample Return Mission, but that mission had its budget completely cut by current US administration who said crewed missions would return the samples instead, presumably in the far distant future.

Plus as a bonus, on the surface of Phobos there should be bits of Mars, that have flown off from asteroid impacts on the martian surface and settled there. So we might get a bit of a two-for-one from the MMX mission and finally have some Martian samples to test on.

Because one of the biggest questions we have in science, is where did life come from? And if there’s any evidence of past or current life in Martian samples, that could help us answer that question. Because either life independently involves on each planet or moon in the universe if the right ingredients and conditions are there, or life could be seeded on planets through impacts with asteroids and comets and all have a common origin.

That idea is known as panspermia. But, this month a paper from Anslow and collaborators has cast some doubt on that idea through the computer simulations they’ve run.

To find out more check out my latest video, and follow along for more about not just what we know in space, but how we know it.

Video filmed on a Sony ⍺7 IV
Video edited by Martino Gasparrini: martino.freelance@gmail.com
Video produced by Marina Hui & Dr Becky Smethurst

I like to focus on how we know things, not just what we know. And especially, the things we still don't know. If you've ever wondered about something in space and couldn't find an answer online - you can ask me! My day job is to do research into how supermassive black holes can affect the galaxies that they live in. items.body:
Visit https://voxelpla.com to check out their super reliable filaments & accessories!
Check out the Prusa Core One INDX: https://geni.us/Prusa-INDX

After more than 10 weeks and almost 40,000 tool changes, I'm sharing my experience with the Prusa CORE One INDX and its eight-tool changing system. While it delivers outstanding multicolor prints with surprisingly little waste, frustrating software, firmware, and design decisions hold it back. In this review, I put the INDX through its paces, explore its strengths and weaknesses, and discuss whether Prusa's open-source approach is worth the compromises.

items.title: Playing with the new touch screen Macs, for science! #shorts
items.summary: Touch screen Macs, everybody’s talking about them, is it useful, is it not? And look, I’m not a tech creator, I’m a scientist. I spend a lot of time working at a computer, running code, making graphs,…
items.body:
Touch screen Macs, everybody’s talking about them, is it useful, is it not? And look, I’m not a tech creator, I’m a scientist. I spend a lot of time working at a computer, running code, making graphs, and looking at images of space taken by professional telescopes.

At least 80% of us astrophysicists are mac users, and that’s a historical thing, OS is a unix based system meaning when it was launched we could run code and simulations, and analyse data, all on the same machine we could do more everyday things like write research papers. Combine that with the fact we’re also an imaging science, and the Macs with their displays win hands down for what we need.

In particular, contrast is a big deal for astronomy, so the difference between the brightest thing in the image, like a star, and the darkest thing, the blackness of space. So when Apple invited me to have a play with the new Macbook Pro’s and see those new OLED displays with their super high contrasts in person I was very excited.

And now they’ve sent me one to try out for myself. I’m gonna see if I notice a difference day to day, and if I find myself actually using that controversial touch screen or not.

For now, I’m gonna set this up and test out how much faster this M5 chip is for running my code, which fits some galaxy spectra. Oo i wonder…

No, you can’t use the touchscreen to move the cursor back in terminal, dammit!

NB: This was not sponsored. Apple sent the Macbook Pro M5 Max to me on loan for 2 months to try out, with no contractual obligation to make content.

---

items.title: ELT's INSANE 39m MIRROR! #shorts
items.summary: Why do we need a telescope as large as 39m across? The bigger the telescope you have, the smaller the object you can see. And thanks to ELT’s size and its 6 giant lasers that can correct for the blurr…
items.body:
Why do we need a telescope as large as 39m across?

The bigger the telescope you have, the smaller the object you can see. And thanks to ELT’s size and its 6 giant lasers that can correct for the blurring of Earth’s atmosphere, ELT should be able to give us images that are 16 times sharper than Hubble, and 6 times sharper than JWST once it comes online in 2030.

But one single piece of glass 39m wide is not a good idea. It would be so heavy that it would bend under its own weight.

Instead engineers have developed ELT’s primary light collecting mirror to have 798 individual hexagonal segments each measuring 1.4 metres across.

That means installing ELT’s mirror is going to be one very large, nervous jigsaw puzzle.

That’s the job of the segment manipulator.

And to see that, we need to head to the heart of engineering at ESO, and get geared up.

In this Seestar S30 Plus review, I share my backyard astrophotography results and explain where it fits between the original Seestar S30 and S30 Pro.

After about a week of testing, I’ve captured the Andromeda Galaxy, Horsehead Nebula, and Sun, tried both alt-az and EQ mode, and explored the separate wide-angle camera. There’s plenty to like about this portable smart telescope, along with a few limitations to understand before buying.

The S30 Plus combines a telescope, cameras, automatic tracking, and live image stacking in one compact setup controlled from your phone. Its dual 2K cameras produce 1440 × 2560 images, offering more resolution than the original S30 while keeping the price below the S30 Pro.

In this video, I cover:

• Seestar S30 Plus vs. S30 vs. S30 Pro: what’s different?
• My deep-sky images and first impressions
• What “dual 2K imaging” actually means
• Alt-az vs. EQ mode and my preferred exposure length
• Choosing the built-in filter for galaxies and nebulae
• Wide-angle Milky Way, star-trail, and time-lapse modes
• Battery performance during cold, damp nights
• Storage, FITS files, and USB transfer quirks
• Solar imaging with the supplied solar filter
• Who should buy the S30 Plus—and whether it’s worth upgrading

items.body:
很多朋友可能第一次听到“大千干烧鱼”这个名字，这里的“大千”指的是国画大师张大千先生。张大千是四川内江人，不仅画画厉害，也非常懂吃、会做川菜。资料记载，大千干烧鱼是在传统川味烧鱼的基础上经过他的改良形成的。这道菜最大的特点就是“干烧”，不留很多汤汁，慢慢把汁水收浓，让味道都挂在鱼上面，吃起来干香浓郁，特别下饭。

【主料】
鲤鱼（1条）

【辅料】
去皮五花肉（一小块）
红泡椒（80克）
生姜（20克）
大蒜（40克）
大葱（1根）
四川菜籽油（150克）
猪油（80克）
明油（少许）

【调味料】
郫县豆瓣酱（8克）
料酒（10克）
酱油（10克）
晒醋（15克）
白糖（20克）
胡椒粉（适量）
食用盐（3克）
味精（3克）
